sections.text: Chemical
Technical Procedure
Title

4500CL Chlorine ( 
 Residual ).
Procedure

Using Standard Method, 
 B. Iodometric Method
14th Edition, 1976, p.96
Introduction

The chlorination of water supplies and polluted waters serves primarily to 
destroy or deactivate disease-producing microorganisms. A secondary benefit, 
particularly in treating drinking water, is the overall improvement in water 
quality.

Chlorination may produce adverse effects. Taste and odor characteristics of 
phenols and other organic compounds present in a water supply may be 
intensified. Carcinogenic chloroform may be formed.

To fulfill the primary purpose of chlorination and to minimize any adverse 
effects, it is essential that proper testing procedures be used with a 
for knowledge of the limitations of the analytical determination.

Chlorine applied in water 
in its molecular or hypochlorite form initially undergoes hydrolysis to form 
free chlorine consisting of aqueous molecular chlorine, hypochlorous acid and 
hypochlorite ion. At the pH of most waters, hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite ion will predominate. Free chlorine reacts with NH3 to form 
combined chlorine.

initiated by chem. Hanaa Rizk Mahmod Shahin reviewed by Chem. Ahmed Matwaly by 
quality control Chemist
Saad Sadeek Hasanen, 
and accepted by eng. Fathy Mahmoud Ragab, 
and approved by Eng: Awad M Fatthy Head Sector of 
Talkha Power Station.

Abd El Gilil EDEPC MPIS coordinator, and certified by accountant; Mahmoud 
Mohamed Soliman; EDEPC admin and financial inspection, quality control General 
Director and supervisor of inspection and quality control head sector.
Significance

The iodometric method "B" is 
suitable for measuring total chlorine concentration for natural and treated waters greater than 1 mg /L but this 
method suffer from interferences.
Summary

Chlorine will liberate free iodine from potassium iodide KI solutions at pH 8 or 
less. The liberated iodine is titrated with a standard solution of sodium 
thiosulfate Na2S2O3 with starch as the 
indicator. Titrate at pH 3 to 4 because the reaction stoichiometric at natural 
pH due to partial oxidation of thiosulfate to sulfate.
Interferences

Oxidized forms of Mn 
interferes.

Reducing agents such as 
organic sulfides also interfere.

The acid titration is preferred because some forms of combined 
chlorine don't react at pH 7. Use only acetic acid for the acid titration; 
sulfuric acid H2SO4 will increase interferences; never use 
hydrochloric acid HCl.

sections.text: Minimum Detectable Concentration

The Minimum detectable concentration approximates 40 g
Cl as Cl2/L if 0.01 N Na2S2O3 is 
used with a 1000-mL sample. Concentrations below 1mg/L cannot be determined 
accurately by this method.
Safety Precautions

Store 
 sample in glass bottles.

The reagent 
 used must be of sufficiently high purity to permit its use without 
 lessening the accuracy of determination.

items:
The reagent 
 used must be of sufficiently high purity to permit its use without 
 lessening the accuracy of determination.

The sample must be taken as the applicable ASTM methods D 
 3370-76.

Acids such as acetic acid and others are dangerous, so you 
 have to wear breathing mask.

Keep 
 these acids closed. Do not get it in the eyes, on the skin, or on clothing. 
 Don't breathe them, use only in a hood.

sections.text:
Tools and 
Equipment
Reagents

Acetic Acid- 
Conc. (glacial).

Potassium Iodide- 
KI, 
crystals.

Standard 
Sodium Thiosulphate Titrant 0.025 N- Dissolve 
6.205 gm of Na2S2O3.5 H2O 
in 100 ml freshly boild distilled water then complete to 1000 ml and standardize against potassium biiodate 
or potassium dichromate after at least 2 weeks storage. This initial storage is 
necessary to allow oxidation of any bisulfite ion present.To saving the solution add 
5 ml chloroform CHCl3 or 0.4 gm of NaOH to minimize 
bacterial decomposition.

Starch 
Indicator Solution- To 5 gm add a little cold 
water and grind in a mortar to a thin paste pour into 1 L of boiling distilled 
water, stir, and let settle over night. Use clear supernate. Note 
for preservation of starch add 1.25 gm of salycilic acid 
and 4 gm of ZnCL2.

Standard 
Iodine Solution 0.1 N- Dissolve 40 gm KI in 25 ml 
chlorinedemand free water, add 13 gm resublimed to a 1-L volumetric flask 
and dilute to mark.

Dilute 
Standard Iodine Titrant 
0.028 N- Dissolve 25 gm KI in a little 
water in a 1-L volumetric flask add correct amount of 0.1 N iodine solution 
exactly standardized to yield a 0.0282 N solution and dilute to 1 L with 
chlorine demand free water.
Work to be Carried out
Procedure
Volume of Sample

Select a sample volume that 
will require no more than 20 ml 0.01N Na2S2O3 and no less than 0.2 mL for the starch iodide end 
point.

For a chlorine range of 1 to 10 mg/L use a 500 
mL sample, above 10 mg/L, use proportionately less sample.

items:
Select a sample volume that 
will require no more than 20 ml 0.01N Na2S2O3 and no less than 0.2 mL for the starch iodide end 
point.

For a chlorine range of 1 to 10 mg/L use a 500 
mL sample, above 10 mg/L, use proportionately less sample.

sections.text:
Preparation 
for Titration

Place 5 mL acetic acid to reduce pH between 3.0 and 4.0 in a flask, add about 1 gm KI, pour sample in and 
mix with a stirring rod.
Titration

Titrate away from direct 
sunlight. Add 0.025 N or 0.01 N Na2S2O3 from 
a buret until the yellow color of the liberated iodine is discharged.
Add 1 mL starch solution and titrate until blue is discharged.

a buret until the yellow color of the liberated iodine is discharged.
Add 1 mL starch solution and titrate until blue is discharged.

sections.text: Blank Titration

Correct result of sample 
titration by determing blank contributed by oxidizing or reducing reagent 
impurities.

Take a volume of distilled 
water corresponding to the sample used for titration, add 5 mL acetic acid, 1gm KI and starch solution.

impurities.

water corresponding to the sample used for titration, add 5 mL acetic acid, 1gm KI and starch solution.

sections.text:
If a blue color develops, titrate with 0.01 N or 0.025 N Na2S2O3 to 
disappearance of blue color and record result ( B is negative ).

If no blue color occurs, 
titrate with 0.0282 N iodine solution until a blue color appears. Backtitration 
with 0.01N or 0.025 N Na2S2O3 and record the 
difference ( B is positive ).

disappearance of blue color and record result ( B is negative ).

If no blue color occurs, 
titrate with 0.0282 N iodine solution until a blue color appears. Backtitration 
with 0.01N or 0.025 N Na2S2O3 and record the 
difference ( B is positive ).

sections.text:
Before calculating the chlorine concentration, substract the blank titration of 
( 1 ) from the sample titration or if necessary add the net equivalent value of the blank 
titration of ( 2 ).
Calculation

For determining total 
available residual chlorine in a water sample
ml Cl as Cl2/L = (AB) X N X 35450
mL sample
Where :

A = 
mL titration 
of sample,

B = 
mL titration 
for blank positive or negative and
N = normality of Na2S2O3.
